title: What Adobe will probably ask for
body:
The statement drops when Round 3 opens on **27 Aug 2026, 04:00 PM IST**, and you have until **13 Sep 2026, 11:59 PM IST**. That is 17 days. Teams that start thinking on day one lose to teams that started building infrastructure in August.

The theme is fixed — *Speak to Agents: The New Language of Brand Visibility* — and Adobe sells measurement and activation tooling to marketers. So the problem will almost certainly sit in the intersection of **agents**, **brand discovery**, and **something a marketer can act on**.

Eight candidate statements, with what a winning solution to each looks like:

1. **"Build a tool that measures a brand's visibility across AI assistants."** Winner: a real prompt-sampling harness with statistical honesty about variance, not a dashboard of invented numbers.
2. **"Help a brand understand *why* it is not being cited."** Winner: stage-level diagnosis — indexed / retrieved / selected / cited / characterised — with a specific fix per stage.
3. **"Build an agent that optimises content for generative retrieval."** Winner: takes a real URL, analyses chunkability and structure, and outputs a rewritten version with a before/after retrieval score.
4. **"Design the interface between a brand and a shopping agent."** Winner: a working product feed plus an MCP server or API an agent can actually query, demoed with a real agent completing a constrained purchase.
5. **"Detect and correct misinformation about a brand in AI answers."** Winner: sentiment extraction, source tracing back to the offending document, and a suggested correction.
6. **"Simulate how an agent chooses between competing brands."** Winner: a transparent scoring model that shows *why* one product won under a given constraint set.
7. **"Make an existing website agent-ready."** Winner: an automated audit — schema coverage, crawler access, heading structure, feed completeness — that emits a prioritised fix list.
8. **"Give marketers a conversational analytics agent."** Winner: natural-language questions over real visibility data, with the caveat that this is the most crowded idea and the hardest to differentiate.

**The through-line:** every winning version measures something real and produces an action. Build the measurement layer now — whatever the statement turns out to be, you will need it.
checklist: Team agrees on which 2 predictions to pre-build toward
Measurement harness started before 27 Aug
Everyone has read the theme brief section of this app

title: A reference architecture you can pre-build
body:
This architecture serves most of the predicted statements. Build the spine now; swap the head later.

```text
                 +------------------+
   prompt panel  |  Prompt Sampler  |  scheduled, multi-engine, N runs per prompt
   (JSON/DB) --> |  (worker/cron)   |
                 +--------+---------+
                          | raw answers + citations
                          v
                 +------------------+
                 |    Extractor     |  brand mentions, positions, cited URLs,
                 |  (LLM + regex)   |  sentiment, claim spans
                 +--------+---------+
                          | structured rows
                          v
                 +------------------+       +------------------+
                 |    Data store    |<----->|  Scoring engine  |  share of voice,
                 | (Postgres + pg   |       |                  |  position weight,
                 |  vector for RAG) |       +--------+---------+  trend, variance
                 +--------+---------+                |
                          |                          v
                          |                 +------------------+
                          |                 | Recommender agent|  reads a losing prompt,
                          |                 |  (ReAct + tools) |  fetches the page, proposes
                          |                 +--------+---------+  a concrete fix
                          v                          |
                 +---------------------------------------------+
                 |               Dashboard (web)               |
                 |  trend, prompt drill-down, competitor set,  |
                 |  fix queue with owner + expected impact     |
                 +---------------------------------------------+
```

**Component notes**

- **Prompt Sampler** — the hard part is honesty. Same locale, clean session, N ≥ 5 runs per prompt per period, and store every raw answer so results are auditable. Judges notice when a demo cannot show its raw data.
- **Extractor** — a hybrid. Regex and string matching for known brand and domain lists (fast, deterministic); an LLM with a strict JSON schema for position, sentiment and claim extraction. Never let the LLM do what a string match can do reliably.
- **Scoring** — position-weighted share of voice (1/position works well), plus a confidence interval. Showing error bars is a differentiator on its own.
- **Recommender agent** — ReAct loop with three tools: `fetch_page`, `analyse_structure`, `propose_rewrite`. This is where you demonstrate agentic engineering rather than a single prompt call.
- **Dashboard** — the fix queue is what makes it a product rather than a report. Every insight must terminate in an action with an owner.
checklist: Sampler stores raw answers, not just parsed scores
Extractor uses deterministic matching where possible
Scores carry a confidence interval
Every insight ends in an actionable item

title: Stack — decide this before the statement drops
body:
Optimise for *shipping in 17 days with 3 people*, not for what would scale to a million users.

| Layer | Pick | Why | Cheaper fallback |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frontend | Next.js + TypeScript + Tailwind | One framework for UI and API routes; deploys to Vercel with zero config | Vite + React, static host |
| Charts | Recharts | Sane defaults, small API surface, quick to style | Hand-rolled SVG |
| Backend | Next.js API routes; Python FastAPI only if you need the data ecosystem | Fewer moving parts beats architectural purity at this timescale | Serverless functions only |
| Database | Postgres via Supabase or Neon | Free tier, real SQL, `pgvector` if you need embeddings | SQLite committed to the repo for a demo-only build |
| Vector store | `pgvector` in the same Postgres | One database is one less thing to break on demo day | In-memory index |
| Scheduling | Vercel Cron or GitHub Actions on a schedule | No infrastructure to run | A script the demo runs manually |
| LLM | One primary provider, one fallback, behind a single interface | Provider outage on demo day is a real risk | Cached fixture responses |
| Auth | Skip it, or Clerk/Supabase Auth if genuinely needed | Auth is a time sink that wins no marks unless multi-tenancy is the point | Hardcoded demo user |
| Hosting | Vercel | Push-to-deploy, free, judges can open a live URL | Netlify |

**Rules that save the project**

- **Every external call goes behind an interface with a cached fixture mode.** `USE_FIXTURES=true` must produce a full working demo with no network. This is the single highest-value engineering decision you will make, and it is what saves you when an API is rate-limited ten minutes before you present.
- **Never commit keys.** Use `.env.local`, commit `.env.example`. A leaked key in a public repo is a real risk and reads as carelessness.
- **Pick the stack the team already knows.** Learning a framework during a hackathon costs more than the framework saves.
- Where it is genuinely relevant, referencing Adobe's ecosystem — Experience Platform data, an Agent Orchestrator-style pattern — earns credibility. Do not bolt it on artificially; judges can tell.
checklist: Stack agreed and scaffolded before 27 Aug
Fixture mode works with the network disabled
.env.example committed, real keys never
Live URL deploys from main on every push

title: Repository standards that actually score
body:
The submission is a GitHub link. A judge spends perhaps ninety seconds on the repo before forming an opinion. Optimise the first screen.

```text
.
├── README.md              <- the whole pitch, above the fold
├── ARCHITECTURE.md        <- diagram + decisions + trade-offs
├── DEMO.md                <- how to run it in under 5 minutes
├── .env.example
├── .gitignore
├── LICENSE                <- MIT unless told otherwise
├── package.json
├── docs/
│   ├── problem-statement.md
│   ├── methodology.md      <- how the metric is computed, and its limits
│   └── screenshots/
├── src/
│   ├── app/                <- routes and UI
│   ├── lib/                <- sampler, extractor, scoring, agent tools
│   └── types/
├── tests/
└── scripts/
    └── seed.ts             <- populates a demo dataset in one command
```

### README template

```markdown
# <Project name>

> One sentence: what it does and who it is for.

**Live demo:** <url>  ·  **Video:** <2-3 min link>  ·  **Team:** names, college

![screenshot](docs/screenshots/hero.png)

## The problem
Two or three sentences. Name the user and what they cannot do today.

## What we built
Three to five bullets, each a capability, not a technology.

## How it works
One diagram plus one paragraph. Link to ARCHITECTURE.md for depth.

## Run it locally
```bash
git clone <repo> && cd <repo>
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # fixture mode needs no keys
npm run dev
```

## What is real and what is mocked
Be explicit. Judges trust honesty far more than they punish scope.

## What we would build next
Three bullets. Shows you know the difference between a demo and a product.
```

**Commit hygiene:** small, present-tense, meaningful messages. `main` always deploys. Feature branches merged by PR even in a team of three — the history is itself evidence of engineering discipline, and judges do look.

**The section that wins trust:** *"What is real and what is mocked."* Almost nobody writes it. It converts a possible accusation into a demonstration of judgement.
checklist: README readable in 60 seconds, screenshot above the fold
Live demo URL in the first three lines
One-command local run that works from a clean clone
'What is real and what is mocked' section present
No secrets in git history

title: The demo
body:
Assume the judge watches three minutes and never installs anything.

**Structure — 3 minutes**

| Time | Beat |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:20 | The problem, in one concrete sentence with a real example. "Ask any assistant which project tool suits a 200-person team. This brand is never mentioned. They cannot see that, and they cannot see why." |
| 0:20–0:40 | What you built, one sentence, then straight into the product. |
| 0:40–2:20 | Live walkthrough of the *single* most impressive path. One path, done fully. Not a tour. |
| 2:20–2:45 | The insight that only your tool produces. This is the moment that gets remembered. |
| 2:45–3:00 | What is next, and the ask. |

**Record it.** A recorded demo with a live URL underneath beats a live demo that fails. Record in fixture mode so it is deterministic, and say on screen that you did.

**Risk control**

- Fixture mode tested with wifi off, the day before.
- Demo data seeded by one command, so a broken database is a 30-second recovery.
- Browser tabs pre-opened, notifications off, screen at a readable resolution.
- No live coding. Ever.

**The most common demo failure** is spending ninety seconds on login, navigation and settings before showing anything interesting. Start the recording on the screen that shows the value. Everything before that is throat-clearing.
checklist: 3-minute recording exists a week before the deadline
Fixture mode verified with the network off
One command seeds demo data
Value visible within the first 30 seconds

title: Supporting documents
body:
The brief says *"the GitHub repository link and any supporting documents"*. Prepare these; they cost little and differentiate a lot.

**1. Solution document (4–6 pages)**
- Problem and who has it
- Your approach, and the alternatives you rejected with reasons
- Architecture diagram
- What you built versus what you designed
- Results or validation, however small
- Limitations, stated plainly
- Roadmap

**2. Methodology note (1–2 pages)** — if your project computes any metric, document exactly how. Sample size, weighting, what is excluded, known biases, confidence. This is the document that separates a serious team from a demo, and almost nobody submits one.

**3. Architecture document** — the diagram plus the three or four decisions that actually mattered, each with the trade-off you accepted. "We chose Postgres with pgvector over a dedicated vector database because one datastore is one less failure mode in a 17-day build; we accept worse recall at scale."

**4. Demo video** — 2–3 minutes, hosted somewhere that will not expire.

**5. Team document** — who did what. Judges ask, and a clear split reads as a functioning team.

**Writing rules:** no marketing language, no invented statistics, no claim you cannot demonstrate. If something is a prototype, call it a prototype. Overclaiming is the fastest way to lose a technically strong submission, because the moment a judge catches one inflated claim they discount everything else.
checklist: Methodology note written for any metric you compute
Every rejected alternative has a stated reason
Limitations section is honest and specific
No claim in the docs that the demo cannot show

title: Seventeen-day execution plan
body:
Round 3 runs 27 Aug – 13 Sep 2026. Three people. Roles are ownership, not silos.

**Before 27 Aug — the free head start**
- Scaffold the repo, deploy a hello-world to Vercel, wire CI.
- Build the prompt sampler and the data model. These are statement-independent.
- Agree the stack, the branch strategy, and who owns what.

**Days 1–3 (27–29 Aug) — lock scope**
- Read the statement together. Write your own one-paragraph restatement and agree on it before touching code.
- Decide the single demo path you will show at the end. Everything is judged against whether it serves that path.
- Cut ruthlessly on day 3. Scope grows; it never shrinks on its own.

**Days 4–9 — build the spine**
- *Engineer A*: data pipeline — sampler, extractor, storage, scoring.
- *Engineer B*: interface — the dashboard and the one path that matters.
- *Engineer C*: the agent layer plus fixture mode and seed scripts.
- **End of day 9: end-to-end works, ugly.** If it does not, cut scope, do not add hours.

**Days 10–13 — make it good**
- Polish the demo path only. Everything off that path stays ugly and that is correct.
- Write the README and the methodology note now, not on day 17.
- First demo recording. It will be bad, which is why you do it now.

**Days 14–16 — harden**
- Fixture mode verified offline. Seed script verified from a clean clone.
- Final recording. Documents finished. Screenshots taken.
- Submit on day 16, not day 17.

**Day 17 — buffer.** Something will go wrong. This day is why it will not matter.

**Scope-cut list, in the order you drop things:** auth → multi-user → settings → mobile layout → historical trends → extra AI engines → export → anything with the word *also* in front of it.
checklist: Repo scaffolded and deployed before 27 Aug
One-paragraph restatement agreed by all three before coding
Single demo path chosen and written down
End-to-end working by day 9
Submitted by day 16

title: How you will be judged, and the artefact that proves each
body:
Hackathon rubrics vary, but they converge on five things. For each, there is one artefact that proves it — build the artefact, not the impression.

| Criterion | What it really means | The artefact that proves it |
|---|---|---|
| **Innovation** | Not "did you use AI" but "did you see something others did not" | One insight your tool surfaces that a spreadsheet could not. Show it in the demo. |
| **Technical depth** | Real engineering, not a wrapper around one API call | The agent loop, the scoring method with its confidence interval, the fixture architecture. ARCHITECTURE.md carries this. |
| **User experience** | Can the intended user get value without you explaining it | The 3-minute recording with no narration crutches; a stranger should follow it. |
| **Impact / relevance** | Does an Adobe customer actually need this | One sentence in the README naming the customer and what it replaces. |
| **Presentation** | Can you explain it under pressure | Rehearsed 3-minute demo, plus a one-page answer to "why this approach and not X". |

**What separates the top ten from the top fifty**, consistently:

1. **The project measures something real.** Invented dashboard numbers are visible from a mile away and judges ask about the data source within the first two questions.
2. **Honesty about limits.** "This samples 120 prompts weekly across two engines; below a 5-point move we cannot distinguish signal from noise" is a stronger statement than any confident claim.
3. **It ends in an action.** Insight without a recommended fix is a report, not a product.
4. **The repo is legible.** A judge who can understand the project from the README alone is a judge who trusts everything else.
5. **One thing done completely** beats five things done partly. Every time.
checklist: Can you name the one insight only your tool produces?
Can you state your method's limits in one sentence?
Does every insight in the UI have an action attached?
Would a stranger understand the project from the README alone?
